Here's the actual arithmetic, on two-number vectors. The query against each key gives a score, and softmax makes them weights. Point four six for trophy. The pronoun's new vector is that blend of the values, pulled toward trophy's. Point the query at suitcase instead, and the blend follows. A different question gets a different answer.

A real model runs many of these side by side, called heads, each with its own idea of relevant. And it stacks them dozens of layers deep. There's a price. Every token scores every other one. Ten tokens make a hundred scores. Double the text, and it's four times the work. So let's put all the pieces in order.

Your text becomes token IDs. Each ID becomes its embedding, plus its position. Then comes a block. Attention mixes information between tokens, then a feed-forward network works on each token alone. Around each half, the input's added back in, so nothing gets lost. And the block repeats. Thirty-two times, in the lesson's mid-sized model.

That model has about seven billion parameters. So where do they live? The embedding table holds half a billion, and the output layer as much again. Attention, about two. The feed-forward networks hold three point eight billion. Fifty-four percent of the whole model. That's where much of what it knows lives. There's no fact database in there. Just weights. Width sets how much one token's vector can hold. Depth sets how many times it gets refined. You need both.

The biggest open models split that feed-forward half into many experts, and run only a few for each token. DeepSeek V3 stores six hundred seventy-one billion parameters, and each token uses thirty-seven billion of them.

And at the very top, the last token's vector becomes one score for every token in the vocabulary. A hundred and twenty-eight thousand scores. Something still has to pick one.
